author: Don Shoopman
title: CCA-Louisiana's Sugar Chapter raises an estimated $159,000 during annual banquet
text:
Nearly 600 outdoorsmen and outdoorswomen filled the Cade Community Center recently for the annual Coastal Conservation Association of Louisiana Sugar Chapter banquet.
The fundraiser lived up to its past on Aug. 20. Banquet-goers who care about preserving or restoring finfish populations along Louisiana’s Gulf Coast turned out again like they have since the first one in 2005.
CCA-Louisiana executive director and CEO Rad Trascher made his way west along Interstate 10 from Baton Rouge once again to St. Martin Parish to enjoy the Sugar Chapter fundraising event that Thursday evening. He enjoyed the experience, one that for the first time in the chapter’s history included live entertainment as Cliff Bernard, a popular musician and acoustic singer from Erath, performed for the crowd.
These silent auction items at the recent CCA-Louisiana Sugar Chapter fundraising event included a “Gulf of America” cap. The silent auction and live auction raised a total of more than $77,000 while the evening’s total raised was $159,000.
FACEBOOK.COM
According to a CCA-Louisiana official, the preliminary estimate for the live and silent auctions was more than $77,000. Also, he said, the raffles brought in $31,000 on a night when approximately $159,000 was raised for CCA-Louisiana.
Trascher was duly impressed.
The Cade Community center was packed with banquet-goers supporting CCA-Louisiana’s Sugar Chapter fundraising event held in mid-August.
SUBMITTED
“It was great to see a packed house at Cade Community Center, showing that the Sugar Chapter is still one of the most impactful chapters of CCA in the state. And they were all excited to hear about the conservation work that CCA is doing these days from reefs to restocking redfish and everything in between. Without support from our local chapters, none of it would be possible,” Trascher said after the banquet.
Another CCA-Louisiana official noted there was a line waiting to get in long before the doors opened at 5:30 p.m. at the Cade Community Center. Anthony Coll, CCA-Louisiana regional director, praised the support and the local Sugar Chapter.
“With a wonderful committee and amazing donations from generous donors and the local community, the night was truly one to remember, not just for the CCA Sugar Chapter but for CCA-Louisiana as a whole,” Coll said later.
CCA-Louisiana’s regional director called it an “exceptional” banquet. He pointed out there were 65 sponsored tables, plus additional tables for walk-ins.
The local spotlight was put on Chris Gondran of Lafayette, formerly of New Iberia. Gondran was recognized for his dedication and efforts as a proud Sugar Chapter member when he received the annual Al Broussard Volunteer of the Year Award. The award is named after the long-time CCA-Louisiana member, Loreauville mayor and avid saltwater angler who died in a head-on crash in 2015.
Corry Landry, a co-founder of the Sugar Chapter, was the first recipient of the award in 2015. At last year’s banquet, the prestigious local award was presented to Ryan Haydel.
Last weekend for snapper?
After this past weekend, recreational red snapper fishermen have one more opportunity at loading the ice chest with the delicacy of the deep after the season was inexplicably, according to many offshore anglers, closed on Aug. 9.
Louisiana’s recreational red snapper season was reopened Aug. 27-30 and will reopen again Sept. 4-7 for the Labor Day Weekend. After Sept. 7, the season will close until further notice.
The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries closed the season the second week of August based on harvest estimates and projections at the time, according to a prepared statement released Aug. 21. The LA Creel data at the time showed approximately 35,109 pounds, or 4 percent, of the state’s 2026 private recreational allocation remains.
The closure caused much consternation among many red snapper anglers across the coast. Some questioned why the season started so early and others wondered about the fifth red snapper added to the daily creel limit on two weekends.
Others point out, correctly, LA Creel is the model program for other Gulf Coast states.
Tradin’ fishin’ poles for shotguns
Some of Acadiana’s outdoorsmen are planning to save the fishin’ rods, at least for a while, and pick up a shotgun as August turns to September. Never mind that it’ll be in the 90s. For them, it’s time to hunt.
Their first chance begins Sept. 5 when Louisiana’s dove hunting season opens for the first split in both the North Zone and the South Zone. North Zone dove hunters will try to get their limit of meals on wings from Sept. 5-27 while dove hunters in the South Zone hope to gun down a few doves from Sept. 5-20.
The North Zone’s second split is Oct. 10-Nov. 15 while the third split is Dec. 19-Jan. 17. South Zone dove hunting dates for the second split are Oct. 17-Nov. 29 and Dec. 12-Jan. 10 for the third split.
Dove hunters 18 and older must have a basic hunting license and be Harvest Information Program certified. Youth 17 and under don’t need a hunting license or HIP certification to hunt doves.
The daily bag limit per person is six and the possession limit is 18. Good luck and safe hunting to all.
DON SHOOPMAN is outdoors editor of The Daily Iberian.
